'''Giorgi Nikoladze'''{{Efn|{{langx|ka|გიორგი ნიკოლაძე|Giorgi Nikoladze}}; {{Langx|ru|Георгий Николаевич Николадзе|Georgy Nikolayevich Nikoladze}};{{Family name footnote|Nikolayevich|[[Nikoladze]]|lang=East Slavic}} {{Langx|fr|Georges Nicoladzé}}; also called "George Nikoladze" in some English-language sources}} (11 August 1888 – 22 September 1931) was a Georgian mathematician, metallurgist, translator, gymnast, and alpinist. He worked as a professor at [[Tbilisi State University]] and as a translator for technical language into Georgian. He was also a cofounder of the [[Georgian Mathematical Union]], founder of the first Georgian gymnastic society ''Shevardeni'', and led a summit to [[Mount Kazbegi]]. 

== Biography ==
The son of writer [[Niko Nikoladze]] and biologist [[Olga Guramishvili-Nikoladze]], and a member of the [[Nikoladze]] noble family, Giorgi Nikoladze was born on 11 August 1888 at {{Ill|Didi Jikhaishi|qid=Q16368349}} in [[Georgia within the Russian Empire|Georgia, then part of the Russian Empire]]. He first studied at the [[First Tbilisi Classical Gymnasium]] from 1898 to 1906, then the [[Saint Petersburg State Institute of Technology]] until 1913, where he was granted a Diploma of Technological Engineer in Metallurgy.{{Sfn|Bamberger|2019|p=36}}<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=G.Nikoladze. Curriculum Vitae |url=https://rmi.tsu.ge/person/nikoladze/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20250608150621/https://rmi.tsu.ge/person/nikoladze/ |archive-date=8 June 2025 |access-date=8 June 2025 |website=Razmadze Mathematical Institute }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last1=O'Connor |first1=J J |last2=Robertson |first2=E F |date=September 2018 |title=Nikoloz Muskhelishvili |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Muskhelishvili/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20250608150640/https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Muskhelishvili/ |archive-date=8 June 2025 |access-date=8 June 2025 |website=MacTutor History of Mathematics }}</ref> He then began working at the Tula Metallurgical Plant, later moving to the [[Donetsk Metallurgical Plant]] in the engineering department, and finally returning to Georgia in 1918.{{Sfn|Bamberger|2019|p=36}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kashakashvili |first1=G. |last2=Yugov |first2=P. |date=1999-12-01 |title=110th anniversary of the births of G.N. Nikoladze and N.V. Kashakashvili |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02463576 |journal=Metallurgist |language=en |volume=43 |issue=12 |pages=536–537 |doi=10.1007/BF02463576 |issn=1573-8892|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

From 1918 to 1928, he worked as a lecturer and then a professor at [[Tbilisi State University]], and was awarded a doctorate from the {{Ill|Faculty of sciences of Paris|lt=faculty of sciences|fr|Faculté des sciences de Paris}} at the [[University of Paris]] in 1928<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> for his dissertation in geometry.{{Sfn|Bamberger|2019|p=39}} Nikoladze was also an avid gymnast who was an adherent of the [[Sokol movement]], founding the first Georgian gymnastic society ''Shevardeni'' in 1918.{{Sfn|Bamberger|2019|p=39-40}} In 1920, he jointly published a "Russian-Georgian and Georgian-Russian dictionary of mathematical terms" with {{Ill|Archil Kharadze|ka|არჩილ ხარაძე}} and [[Nikoloz Muskhelishvili]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> With this and other translation projects, Nikoladze sought to establish a uniform technical language in [[Georgian language|Georgian]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Portnoy |first=Esther |date=1975-08-01 |title=Georgii Nikolaevich Nikoladze: By A.N. Bogolyubov. Moscow ("Nauka"), 1973. 166 p |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0315-0860%2875%2990084-1 |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=349 |doi=10.1016/0315-0860(75)90084-1 |issn=0315-0860|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Alongside Kharadze, Muskhelishvli, and [[Andrea Razmadze]], he founded the [[Georgian Mathematical Union]] in 1923.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sharikadze |first=Jondo |url=https://rmi.tsu.ge/muskhelishvili120/Files/Conference2011_Internet.pdf#page=11 |title=Continuum mechanics and related problems of analysis |year=2011 |location=Tbilisi |page=11 |chapter=Nikoloz Muskhelishvili – Scientist and Public Figure}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Duduchava |first1=Roland |last2=Natroshvili |first2=David |last3=Gogishvili |first3=Guram |date=2018-11-30 |title=Georgian Mathematical Union: History and Activity |url=https://ems.press/journals/mag/articles/15900 |journal=European Mathematical Society Magazine |volume=2018-12 |language=en |issue=110 |pages=45–47 |doi=10.4171/news/110/14 |issn=2747-7894|doi-access=free }}</ref> Nikoladze also had a long-time interest in alpinism since his childhood,{{Sfn|Bamberger|2019|p=41}} and in August that same year, he successfully led an expedition to the summit of the 5000-meter high [[Mount Kazbek|Mount Kazbegi]].{{Sfn|Bamberger|2019|p=29}} He was married to Georgetta Gambashidze.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pantsulaia |first=Giorgi |title="Do you serve the nation?" – "Forever!" (Niko Nikoladze's descendants) |url=https://kutaisi.travel/en/11641/do-you-serve-the-nation-forever-niko-nikoladzes-descendants/ |website=Kutaisi|date=10 January 2025 }}</ref> He died on 22 September 1931 in [[Tbilisi]].<ref name=":0" />

== Legacy ==
Although Nikoladze was little-known outside the Soviet Union, he was described as "one of the founders of the mathematics section at Tiflis [Tbilisi], and a pioneer in the technical and scientific development of the Caucasus."<ref name=":1" /> A monumental bust dedicated to him stands in the Giorgi Nikoladze Memorial Square in [[Zestaponi]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lush |first=Emily |date=2024-04-29 |title=10 Things to Do in Zestafoni, Georgia: Soviet Mosaics & More |url=https://wander-lush.org/things-to-do-in-zestafoni-guide/ |access-date=2025-06-08 |website=Wander-Lush |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2016, Georgian historian Paata Natsvlishvili hypothesized that Nikoladze was actually the "[[unknown French boy]]" who won gold at the [[1900 Summer Olympics]] in Paris. According to Natsvlishvili, Nikoladze's sister had told him in an interview in the 1980s that her brother had won a boat race in France, and that the family had been touring Europe at the time of the Olympics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Natsvlishvili |first=Paata |date=2016 |title=Was the "unknown French boy" in 1900 actually from Georgia? |url=https://library.olympics.com/Default/doc/SYRACUSE/2954107/was-the-unknown-french-boy-in-1900-actually-from-georgia-by-paata-natsvlishvili |journal=Journal of Olympic History |series= |language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Natsvlishvili |first=Paata |title=Giorgi Nikoladze : "unknown french boy" |date=2016 |url=https://library.olympics.com/Default/doc/SYRACUSE/207298/giorgi-nikoladze-unknown-french-boy-paata-natsvlishvili |access-date=2025-06-08 |publisher=Georgian Sports Journalists Association |language=English}}</ref> However, some historians from the International Society of Olympic Historians remained unconvinced that Nikoladze was really the unknown boy owing to the circumstantial evidence. Historian [[Bill Mallon]] said that the unknown boy only looked "a little" like Nikoladze.<ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last=Robinson |first=Joshua |date=2016-08-09 |title=This Boy Might Be the Youngest Ever Olympian—No One Knows Who He Is |url=http://www.wsj.com/articles/maybe-eight-possibly-frenchthe-search-for-the-youngest-ever-olympian-1470758952 |access-date=2025-06-08 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>
